Header text located before each exercise, not simply the nearest header on its page. In particular p.38 Q7 belongs to Unique Progressive School, not Sherpur whose next paper begins below Q11.

Assistant-prepared narrative-order and matching keys, not official answers. Coherent alternatives may be accepted by teachers. Original grammar/typos preserved, including guests plural, Donation blood exercise not registered, wondered/wondering, and incomplete tax-collector story ending before the honesty test is explained.

Rearranging examples are literary/fable narratives, not verified historical biographies. Donkey/jackal stories contain animal mistreatment by characters; this is not endorsed. Ferdousi payment is a traditional anecdote, not historical certification. Bayazid narrative has a missing transition from the request to fetching water; retained rather than silently adding a sentence.

Original matching source grammar/punctuation retained, including humanitarian activities. and person who possess. Generalisations and religious descriptions are source claims, not independently certified. Facebook exercise is reading/language practice, not a platform endorsement or universal statement about teenagers.

Held repeated Saadi robbers, Androcles, Napoleon, Keats, Taimur, farming-youth, morality and punctuality sets. Held malformed Globalization/illiteracy combinations, repeated indistinguishable friendship C rows, Lear kingdom-third inconsistency, Maugham play-title errors, historical Akbar/Nazrul ambiguities, medical blood-donation/dengue absolutes and gender-stereotype matching. No silent repairs or auto-approval.

Added ten distinct story scenarios and ten distinct dialogues from school papers. Writing prompt page images separately checked; original writing question numbers and fifteen marks retained (Naogaon stress dialogue is Q10, not Q11). Story answers have a title, original beginning and exactly ten authored continuation sentences. Answers are illustrative, not official or canonical.

Bear escape is explicitly a fable, not wildlife safety guidance. Boatman continuation uses life jackets and sheltered landing instead of endorsing drowning or class-based ridicule. Bayazid continuation chooses practical care and rest rather than prescribing sleeplessness. Azam Shah is presented as a traditional account, not certified history.

Cricket conversation is a fictional match, not a report of an actual event. Price-hike dialogue makes no unverified current price claims. Banking requirements deliberately depend on age, bank and applicable rules; no invented required balance, interest rate or guaranteed eligibility. Mental-health content is general educational content and encourages trusted/professional support. Facebook is distinct from the already registered generic mobile-phone topic; no promotion or assumed underage eligibility.

Repeated factory-fire, Romana locked door, moneybag, thirsty crow, Saadi, Midas, Bruce, Hamelin, railway, lottery, drowning, mobile/newspaper/exercise and future-plan prompts were not counted as new writing stock.

Two additional rearranging sets checked on PDF pp.61 and65: unpaid-letter parcel joke and farmer/horse changing fortunes. Their keys are possible coherent narrative orders, not instructions to post unpaid parcels or a prediction about luck.
All school header years are 2025 except the Akij Facebook dialogue: its header explicitly says Test 2024. This is not reassigned to the compilation target year.

items.topic: There lived a shepherd boy/cow boy

tasks.instruction: Read the beginning of the story. Add at lest ten new sentences to complete the story. Give a suitable title to it. There lived a shepherd boy/cow boy in a certain village. He used to gaze a flock of sheep near a forest. It was not very far from his village. Besides his usual duty he sang and played flute. But the boy had a bad habit. He used to tell a lie.........
tasks.answer:
The Price of a False Alarm
There lived a shepherd boy/cow boy in a certain village. He used to gaze a flock of sheep near a forest. It was not very far from his village. Besides his usual duty he sang and played flute. But the boy had a bad habit. He used to tell a lie.........
One afternoon he shouted that a wolf was attacking his sheep. The villagers hurried from their work to help him. When they arrived, they found no wolf and heard the boy laughing. They warned him that a false alarm wasted precious time. Nevertheless, he played the same trick again a few days later. Then a real wolf appeared near the flock. The frightened boy called urgently for help, but the villagers thought it was another trick. By the time an adult noticed the danger, several sheep had scattered and one was lost. The boy confessed his lies and apologised to everyone he had deceived. He understood that rebuilding trust would require honest behaviour over time.

items.school: SOS Hermann Gmeiner College, Dhaka

tasks.instruction: Read the beginning of the story and complete it in your own words with a suitable title. There were two friends. They lived in a certain village. They promised that they would help each other at the time of danger. One day they were passing through a deep forest. Suddenly, they saw a bear.......
tasks.answer:
Friendship in Danger
There were two friends. They lived in a certain village. They promised that they would help each other at the time of danger. One day they were passing through a deep forest. Suddenly, they saw a bear.......
One friend ran to a nearby tree and climbed it without looking back. The other could not climb and found himself alone on the path. In this old fable, he lay still and pretended to be dead. The bear approached, sniffed him and eventually wandered away. Once the bear had gone, the first friend climbed down. He jokingly asked what the bear had whispered in his companion’s ear. The other replied that it had warned him against friends who abandoned him in danger. The joke vanished as the first friend realised how frightened his companion had been. He apologised for thinking only of himself. The tale teaches loyalty, but its imaginary escape should not be treated as real advice about encountering wild bears.

tasks.instruction: Read the beginning of a story. Add at least ten new sentences to complete the story. Give a suitable title for it. Once there was a small boy named Bayazid. His mother was ill. One night he was studying by the side of his mother's bed. All of a sudden she woke up, raised her head, and told her son to give a glass of water........
tasks.answer:
Care for a Mother
Once there was a small boy named Bayazid. His mother was ill. One night he was studying by the side of his mother's bed. All of a sudden she woke up, raised her head, and told her son to give a glass of water........
Bayazid reached for the water pot but found it empty. He fetched fresh drinking water and returned quietly to the room. By then his mother had fallen asleep again. He placed the covered glass safely beside her bed. Not wanting to disturb her, he sat nearby and continued his reading. A little later she woke and asked whether he had brought the water. Bayazid helped her sit comfortably and handed her the glass. She drank some water and thanked him for his care. He asked if she needed anything else before he went to rest. His thoughtful attention showed that love could be expressed through simple, practical kindness.

items.school: Rajbari Govt. High School, Rajbari

tasks.instruction: Read the beginning of a story. Write at least ten sentences to complete the story. Gias Uddin Azam Shah was a great ruler of Bengal. He was very kind and just. He was fond of hunting. One day he went a hunting at a nearby jungle. He aimed at a fawn but.....
tasks.answer:
Equal Before the Law
Gias Uddin Azam Shah was a great ruler of Bengal. He was very kind and just. He was fond of hunting. One day he went a hunting at a nearby jungle. He aimed at a fawn but.....
The arrow missed its target and struck a young man nearby. The king immediately stopped the hunt and called for help. When he learned that the young man had died, he was filled with grief. The dead man’s mother brought a complaint before the judge. The judge summoned the king just as he would summon any other person. Azam Shah appeared before the court without demanding special treatment. He accepted responsibility and listened respectfully to the grieving mother. The court considered her complaint and ordered redress according to its law. The king obeyed the judgement and praised the judge’s independence. In this traditional account, justice mattered more than the power or rank of the accused.

tasks.instruction: Read the beginning of a story. Add a suitable title and complete the story in your own words. Once upon a time, there lived a boatman in a village beside a river. He was poor and illiterate. So, he was used to rowing in boat from dawn to dusk only to make his both ends meet........................
tasks.answer:
Different Kinds of Knowledge
Once upon a time, there lived a boatman in a village beside a river. He was poor and illiterate. So, he was used to rowing in boat from dawn to dusk only to make his both ends meet........................
One day a scholar hired his boat to cross the river. During the journey the scholar asked whether the boatman knew grammar and philosophy. The boatman replied that he had never had the opportunity to study those subjects. The scholar foolishly mocked him instead of respecting his skill. Suddenly a strong wind rose and water began entering the boat. The boatman calmly asked the passenger to put on the life jacket kept beside him. He then guided the boat towards a sheltered landing. On reaching the bank, the scholar thanked him for bringing them to safety. He apologised for looking down on knowledge acquired through practical experience. Both men agreed that formal learning and practical skills deserved respect.

items.school: Bonowary Lal Govt. High School, Sirajganj
items.topic: Once upon a time a dog

tasks.instruction: Read the beginning of the story and complete it in your own words. Once upon a time a dog was very hungry he went to a butcher's shop and soon stole a big piece of meat. He ran to eat it. He wanted to enjoy the piece of meat alone. In a short while, he reached a stream. The dog began to cross the bridge. In the middle of ..........................
tasks.answer:
A Reflection and a Regret
Once upon a time a dog was very hungry he went to a butcher's shop and soon stole a big piece of meat. He ran to eat it. He wanted to enjoy the piece of meat alone. In a short while, he reached a stream. The dog began to cross the bridge. In the middle of ..........................
The dog looked down and saw his reflection in the clear water. He mistook it for another dog carrying another piece of meat. His greed made him want both pieces for himself. He opened his mouth to bark at the imaginary rival. At once his own piece fell into the stream. The current carried it beyond his reach. He stared into the water but could no longer see any meat. Only then did he realise that he had been fooled by his reflection. He walked away hungry and regretted both his theft and his greed. The fable reminds us that wanting everything can cost us what we already have.

items.school: Saleha Ishaque Govt. Girl's High School, Sirajganj

tasks.instruction: Read the beginning of the story and complete it in your own words. A lion was drinking water from a brook. At the same time, a lamb was also taking water from the down stream of the same brook............
tasks.answer:
An Unjust Accusation
A lion was drinking water from a brook. At the same time, a lamb was also taking water from the down stream of the same brook............
The lion accused the lamb of making his drinking water muddy. The lamb politely explained that the stream flowed from the lion towards him. He could not have dirtied water that was upstream. Unable to answer this, the lion accused him of speaking rudely the previous year. The lamb replied that he had not even been born then. The lion grew angry because each excuse had been shown to be false. In this possible continuation, a shepherd nearby heard their voices and called his dogs. The lion withdrew rather than face the approaching group. The shepherd led the lamb back to the flock. The lamb had spoken truthfully, but timely support had protected him from an abuse of power.

items.topic: One day a crow stole a piece of meat.

tasks.instruction: Read the beginning of the story and write it in your won way. Give a title of it. One day a crow stole a piece of meat. It flew away and sat on the branch of a tree. Suddenly a fox ...........
tasks.answer:
Beware of Flattery
One day a crow stole a piece of meat. It flew away and sat on the branch of a tree. Suddenly a fox ...........
The fox saw the meat in the crow’s beak and wanted it for himself. He stopped beneath the tree and praised the crow’s shiny feathers. The crow listened with pleasure but kept his beak closed. The fox then claimed that such a beautiful bird must have a wonderful voice. He begged the crow to sing just one song. Proud of the praise, the crow opened his beak to caw. The meat fell straight to the ground. The fox snatched it and ran away. The crow realised that the compliments had been intended to deceive him. He regretted his theft and learned to question praise that came with a hidden request.

items.school: Kurigram Govt. Girls' High School, Kurigram
items.topic: Once a hungry fox was searching

tasks.instruction: Read the beginning of the following story. This story is not complete. Write at least ten new sentences to complete the story. Once a hungry fox was searching for food in the forest. After a while, he came to a vineyard. He was very tempted at the sight of the grapes. But the grapes were hanging very high.....................
tasks.answer:
The Sour Grapes
Once a hungry fox was searching for food in the forest. After a while, he came to a vineyard. He was very tempted at the sight of the grapes. But the grapes were hanging very high.....................
He stood beneath a fine bunch and jumped towards it. His mouth closed on nothing but air. He stepped back and tried again with a longer run. Once more the grapes remained beyond his reach. After several attempts he became tired and stopped. He looked around as though he had never wanted the fruit. Then he announced that the grapes were probably sour anyway. He walked away without tasting a single grape. His words did not prove anything about the fruit. The fable shows how people sometimes dismiss what they cannot obtain instead of admitting disappointment.

items.school: Lalmonirhat Govt. High School, Lalmonirhat
items.topic: Once there lived a wood cutter.

tasks.instruction: Read the beginning of the following story. Add at least ten new sentences to complete the story. Once there lived a wood cutter. He was very poor but honest. He lived on the bank of a river. He used to cut wood............
tasks.answer:
The Honest Woodcutter
Once there lived a wood cutter. He was very poor but honest. He lived on the bank of a river. He used to cut wood............
One morning his axe slipped from his hands and fell into the deep river. He sat on the bank, worried because it was the tool he needed for work. In this familiar folktale, a mysterious helper appeared and asked why he was sad. After hearing the explanation, the helper brought a golden axe from the water. The woodcutter said honestly that it did not belong to him. He also refused a silver axe for the same reason. At last the helper showed him his own iron axe. The woodcutter recognised it at once and thanked the helper. Pleased by his honesty, the helper offered the other axes as gifts. The woodcutter returned home knowing that he had not traded his integrity for wealth.

tasks.instruction: You want to know the effects of deforestation. Now, Write a dialogue between You and Your friend about deforestation and its effect.
tasks.answer:
Me: Why are you concerned about deforestation?
Friend: Removing forests can destroy habitats and threaten the plants and animals that depend on them.
Me: Does it affect people too?
Friend: Yes. Forest loss can harm livelihoods, disturb water cycles and increase soil erosion.
Me: What is its connection with climate change?
Friend: Trees store carbon, and clearing or burning forests can release carbon dioxide.
Me: Is planting a few trees enough to replace an old forest?
Friend: No. Protecting existing forests and restoring diverse native habitats are also important.
Me: What can we do as students?
Friend: Reduce unnecessary paper use, learn about responsible sourcing and support properly supervised local conservation.
Me: We should also respect the rights and knowledge of communities living in forests.
Friend: Certainly. Conservation works best when those communities help shape it.

tasks.instruction: Education is the backbone of a nation. No nation can reach its goal without giving priority to it. Suppose, your friend Asif wants to know more about the importance of education. Now, write a dialogue between you and your friend about it.
tasks.answer:
Asif: Why do people call education the backbone of a nation?
Me: It helps people understand the world, develop skills and take part in society.
Asif: Is education only about examination results?
Me: No. It should also encourage curiosity, critical thinking and respect for others.
Asif: How can it improve everyday life?
Me: Reading, numeracy and practical knowledge help people make informed decisions and pursue opportunities.
Asif: Does everyone have the same opportunity to learn?
Me: Unfortunately not. Poverty, disability, distance and discrimination can create barriers.
Asif: Then schools need to be accessible and welcoming.
Me: Yes, and teachers need support, useful materials and a safe environment for teaching.
Asif: We can help classmates respectfully without making them feel inferior.
Me: Exactly. Education is a shared opportunity, not a reason to look down on anyone.

tasks.instruction: Write a dialogue between two friends on exciting cricket match.
tasks.answer:
Friend One: Did you watch yesterday’s school cricket match?
Friend Two: Yes! Our team needed eight runs from the final over.
Friend One: I thought we would lose when the first two balls produced no runs.
Friend Two: Then Rafi hit a four into the gap between two fielders.
Friend One: The next two balls brought only two runs.
Friend Two: That left two runs needed from the last ball.
Friend One: The batter played it gently and both players ran quickly.
Friend Two: They completed the second run just before the wicketkeeper broke the stumps.
Friend One: Both teams shook hands afterwards. I liked that part as much as the finish.
Friend Two: So did I. The losing team had fielded very well.
Friend One: Our coach said teamwork and fair play mattered more than mocking the opponents.
Friend Two: It was an exciting imaginary match to describe, and a good lesson in sportsmanship.

tasks.instruction: Suppose, you are Robin and your friend Rafeed. Now, make a dialogue between you and your friend about the recent price hike of essential commodities in Bangladesh.
tasks.answer:
Robin: Rafeed, families in our neighbourhood are worried about the price of essential goods.
Rafeed: Higher prices can make it difficult to afford food, transport and other necessities.
Robin: What can cause prices to rise?
Rafeed: Possible causes include supply disruptions, increased production costs and changes in import costs.
Robin: So we should not assume one cause explains every price change.
Rafeed: Exactly. Reliable data are needed before blaming particular groups.
Robin: What can authorities do?
Rafeed: Monitor markets fairly, improve supply systems and enforce laws against proven manipulation.
Robin: Targeted support for households with low incomes can help too.
Rafeed: Yes. Consumers can compare prices and avoid unnecessary waste where possible.
Robin: But budgeting alone cannot solve a family’s shortage of income.
Rafeed: True. Lasting solutions require sound policy and reliable access to essential goods.

tasks.instruction: Suppose, you are Rassel. Your friend is Sami. Now, make a dialogue between you and your friend about stress management on exam hall.
tasks.answer:
Rassel: Sami, I become so nervous in the examination hall that I forget what I know.
Sami: That sounds difficult. Have you spoken with a teacher or another trusted adult?
Rassel: Not yet. What could help me during the examination?
Sami: Read the instructions slowly and begin with a question you understand.
Rassel: I sometimes worry about the whole paper at once.
Sami: Try dividing the available time among the sections and focus on one task at a time.
Rassel: What if my thoughts start racing?
Sami: Pause briefly, relax your shoulders and breathe gently at a comfortable pace.
Rassel: I should practise timed questions before the examination too.
Sami: Yes, and protect your sleep rather than studying through the night.
Rassel: If the anxiety keeps disrupting my work, I will ask for support.
Sami: Good idea. A qualified professional can help when anxiety becomes persistent or overwhelming.

tasks.instruction: Suppose, you are Habib/Habiba. You want to open a bank account and keep your scholarship money in it. You have gone to a bank as a client and had a talk with the Manager of the bank. Now, write a dialogue between you and the Manager of the bank.
tasks.answer:
Habib: Good morning. I would like information about opening an account for my scholarship money.
Manager: Welcome. First, may I ask your age so we can explain which account options are suitable?
Habib: I am a school student. Would I need a parent or guardian?
Manager: The requirements depend on your age, the account type and the rules currently applicable.
Habib: What documents should I bring?
Manager: We will give you the official checklist for identity, student status and any guardian documentation required.
Habib: Are there charges or minimum-balance requirements?
Manager: Please read the current schedule of charges and account conditions before deciding.
Habib: Can my scholarship be paid directly into the account?
Manager: We can explain that after checking the scholarship provider’s payment requirements.
Habib: How can I keep the account secure?
Manager: Never share a PIN, password or one-time code, and contact the bank through verified channels if anything seems wrong.

tasks.instruction: Suppose, you are Tabid/Tuhin. Your friend is Rohan/Runa. Now, write a dialogue between you and your friend about the merits and demerits of city and village life.
tasks.answer:
Tabid: Rohan, what do you enjoy about living in a village?
Rohan: I enjoy the familiar community and open spaces, though villages differ greatly.
Tabid: In my city, many schools, workplaces and services are close by.
Rohan: But traffic, pollution and expensive housing can make city life difficult.
Tabid: Yes. What challenges do people in your area face?
Rohan: Some travel far for specialist healthcare or further education.
Tabid: Not every village lacks services, and not every city resident can easily afford them.
Rohan: Exactly. We should avoid treating either place as entirely good or bad.
Tabid: Better transport and reliable internet could widen opportunities in rural areas.
Rohan: Cities also need safe housing, green spaces and accessible public services.
Tabid: People should be able to choose where to live without losing essential opportunities.
Rohan: I agree. Both places deserve thoughtful development and respect.

tasks.instruction: Suppose you are Noha and your friend is Mahin. Now, write a dialogue between you and your friend about the merits and demerits of using Facebook at teenage.
tasks.answer:
Noha: Mahin, what do you think about teenagers using Facebook?
Mahin: Where use is permitted by the platform’s current rules, it can help people communicate and share useful information.
Noha: A supervised study group might help classmates exchange assignments.
Mahin: Yes, but we must check information rather than assume every post is true.
Noha: Spending too much time scrolling can interrupt study and sleep.
Mahin: Notifications and social pressure can make it difficult to stop.
Noha: What safety precautions should users take?
Mahin: Protect personal information, review privacy settings and never share passwords or one-time codes.
Noha: What should someone do about harassment or suspicious messages?
Mahin: Save relevant evidence where safe, use reporting tools and seek support from a trusted adult.
Noha: We should also ask permission before posting another person’s picture.
Mahin: Certainly. No one should feel forced to use social media to remain part of a friendship.

tasks.instruction: Suppose, you are Taufa. You have seen that many people are still illiterate in our country. Now, write a dialogue between you and your friend Mithila regarding how to remove illiteracy problem from Bangladesh.
tasks.answer:
Taufa: Mithila, how can we support people who have not had the chance to learn reading and writing?
Mithila: We should begin by listening to their needs and respecting their experience.
Taufa: Poverty and leaving school early can limit learning opportunities.
Mithila: Distance, inaccessible teaching and family responsibilities can be barriers too.
Taufa: Would flexible adult-literacy classes help?
Mithila: Yes, especially when trained teachers use practical materials in a language learners understand.
Taufa: The timetable should suit work and caring responsibilities.
Mithila: Libraries and community centres could provide safe, accessible places to learn.
Taufa: What can students do responsibly?
Mithila: Help a supervised programme, share suitable books and never embarrass anyone for making a mistake.
Taufa: Keeping children in inclusive schools is important as well.
Mithila: Exactly. Literacy opportunities should be available throughout life.

tasks.instruction: Unemployment is one of the serious problems of Bangladesh. Now, write a dialogue between you and your friend Samira about the unemployment problem and its solution.
tasks.answer:
Me: Samira, why is unemployment such a concern?
Samira: It can cause financial insecurity and make it difficult for people to use their abilities.
Me: What factors can contribute to it?
Samira: A shortage of suitable jobs, economic disruption and mismatches between training and available work are possible factors.
Me: So it is unfair to assume that every unemployed person simply lacks effort.
Samira: Certainly. Many people search hard but face barriers beyond their control.
Me: What kinds of measures could help?
Samira: Better job information, relevant training and fair recruitment can improve access to opportunities.
Me: Businesses also need conditions that support sustainable job creation.
Samira: Yes, alongside safe working conditions and protection against discrimination.
Me: Self-employment may suit some people, but loans and business risks need careful assessment.
Samira: Agreed. There is no single solution, and policies should be assessed using reliable evidence.

The neighbours cried, "Your son broke his leg, what terrible luck!" The farmer replied, "Maybe so, maybe not."
